newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodians mourn bomb attack on opposition protest.
newsitem.headline: Cambodians mourn bomb attack on opposition protest.

text.p: Cambodians on Monday mourned the victims of a weekend grenade attack on an opposition protest that killed at least 14 people while the Interior Ministry said it was still unclear who was responsible.

The attack outside the National Assembly in central Phnom Penh on Sunday morning was the worst and most blatant act of political violence to hit Cambodia's fragile democracy since the current coalition government came to power after United Nations-organised general elections in May 1993.

Protest leader and apparent target Sam Rainsy, who narrowly escaped injury, on Sunday blamed the attack on his bitter foe, co-Premier Hun Sen, but a spokesman for the Information Ministry said it was unclear who was responsible and that an investigation was underway.

"Until now police have found no clues as to who was responsible," Interior Ministry spokesman Sok Phal said. "The Ministry of Interior has started a thorough investigation to discover the perpetrators and those behind them." Hun Sen and First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh had agreed to establish a joint committee to "investigate the incident immediately", said Om Yentieng, an aide to Hun Sen.
Ly Thuch, an advisor to Ranariddh, said: "There is a committee set up in the Ministry of Interior and supported by the two prime ministers to carry out the investigation."
Information Ministry Secretary of State Khieu Kanharith appealed to anyone who had filmed or photographed the attack to assist in the investigation.

A witness said four grenades were thrown from a car that sped past the protest, but Rainsy said at least one was thrown from inside the Assembly compound, in the heart of the capital just metres (yards) from the gates of the royal palace.
There were conflicting reports as to the number killed.
Doctors at the three major hospitals in Phnom Penh that took in casualties said nine people had died in hospital or arrived there dead. Police said on Sunday that seven died at the scene.
The chairman of parliament, Loy Sim Chheang, issued a statement condemning the attack on what he said was a legal protest and put the death toll at 14 with more than 100 injured.
Rainsy put the death toll at 16 while a spokesman for the royalist FUNCINPEC party that rules in an uneasy coalition with Hun Sen's Cambodian People's Party (CPP) put it as high as 20.
Loy Sim Chheang's statement said the government must bring those responsible to justice.
"This recent crime shows that our Kingdom of Cambodia still uses violence against innocent people which is increasing in brutality," it said.
Khieu Kanharith said Hun Sen and Ranariddh had declared a period of national mourning and ordered flags to be flown at half mast though only one or two were seen lowered.

On Monday, mourners lay flowers and burnt incense at the scene. The pavement outside the assembly was still stained with blood and littered with the footwear and scraps of clothing of some of the victims.
On Sunday Hun Sen blamed the attack on terrorists and demanded an immediate investigation. But he also said those responsible for the demonstration should be arrested.
Sunday's protest was against what Rainsy termed the dominance of the judiciary by the CPP.
Sam Rainsy's wife Tioulong Saumura called it only the latest attempt on her husband's life.

"He has been constantly under threat," she told Reuters, adding that FUNCINPEC was sufficiently concerned about Rainsy's safety to send 20 armed policemen to guard his residence and the headquarters of his Khmer Nation Party.

Sam Rainsy became a leading opposition figure and Hun Sen's strongest critic after being fired as finance minister in 1994. He was expelled from parliament in 1995 and his party is not recognised by the government.
It recently formed an alliance with Ranariddh's royalists.
